newsitem.title: USA: States threaten to leave tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: States threaten to leave tobacco talks.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Legal Correspondent

State attorneys general said Tuesday they were ready to walk away from tobacco negotiations if the industry refused to be regulated by the Food and Drug Administration and punished for past wrongdoing.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told reporters that talks would continue through the afternoon but that negotiations have grown very contentious.
Moore said the last two days of talks have been "rocky, hard, tough, brutal, sometimes mean, and today was one of those days."
Earlier in the day, the negotiations appeared near collapse when the industry refused to give in on key issues of FDA regulation and punitive damages.

Moore said emphatically that the attorneys general would walk away from the table if the following three demands were not met: Punishment for past wrongdoing, liability for compensatory and punitive damages and agreement on FDA regulation of nicotine as a drug.

"If we don't get it, we're going home and we're going to try our cases," said Moore, whose state is one of 38 suing cigarette companies to recover the costs of treating diseases allegedly caused by smoking. "This industry ought to be treated like every other industry in America: They ought to be liable for compensatory damages in the future and they ought to be liable for punitive damages in the future," Moore said. "We also believe the FDA ought to regulate nicotine as a drug."
Moore said the attorneys general would never agree to any immunity for the industry.
He said while negotiations would continue this afternoon, "the deadline is pretty near."
Talks between tobacco industry representatives and the state attorneys general have been going on since early April.
The most contentious issue was FDA regulation, Moore said.
"We are not going to give in on that no matter what they say or do," he said.

Although it had appeared the two sides were close to a deal last week, B.A.T Industries, Plc, the parent company of Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., objected to language concerning FDA regulation and encouraged the other companies not to give in.

The attorneys general had been optimistic about reaching a final deal this week and getting a draft proposal to the White House. One of the options they considered was presenting an incomplete proposal with the punitive damage issue still unresolved.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Clinton wanted an agreement that would implement his policies to restrict children's access to tobacco products and that this will "require some process of examination on our part" of any tobacco agreement.
"But it's hard for us to evaluate something that is not concrete and substantive in nature," he said.

As for fears of attorneys general that the White House might not support an agreement if one were reached, McCurry said, "The issue is whether or not they are going to be able to reach an agreement with the parties, and we can't write that agreement for them."

The industry has made numerous concessions in the health area, including an agreement to make sharp cutbacks in advertising and to pay penalties if youth smoking does not decrease over a certain period of time. The industry also has said it will agree to pay for smoking cessation programmes and devices.

The 38 state attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry to recover Medicaid costs of smokers. Mississippi's case is scheduled to be the first to go to trial July 7, with Florida to follow in August.
Both Moore and Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth have said they had no intention of delaying their trials.
"I feel good. We've done everything we can," Butterworth said. "We have fulfilled our responsibility to the states and the country."
